In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
FPD/AML should be considered a genetic disorder with variable phenotypic expression.
the presence of the t(21;21) translocation in a RUNX1 carrier, even if it is de novo, should be considered a risk factor for FPD/AMLF.

FPD/AML should be considered in patients with a history of AML and/or a RUNX1 translocated in a derivative chromosome, and that a RUNX1 abnormality should be looked for in patients with a clinical history of AML or FPD/AML and/or in patients with a RUNX1 rearranged derivative chromosome, even if they have never been diagnosed with FPD/AML.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the presence of a RUNX1 abnormality in a patient should lead to a careful search for a carrier parent and/or sibling, as the presence of the RUNX1 abnormalities may have implications for the patient, the siblings and the offspring.

the RUNX1 translocations are the most frequent genetic abnormalities in FPD/AMD, but they are also the most heterogeneous.
The main takeaway from our work is that
RUNX1 mutations should always be considered in the differential diagnosis of patients with FPD/AML and that the clinical phenotype is highly variable.
RUNX1 mutations can be transmitted through the germ line, but that they can also arise de novo, and in either case they may result in FPD or AML.
